targetSkill: Teach the student to monitor their own comprehension while reading — to notice when meaning breaks down — and to deploy a specific strategy (annotation, re-read, identify the confusion, ask a question, apply SOAPSTone) to recover understanding. The student is not passively reading and hoping; the student is actively tracking comprehension and intervening when it fails.
mustHave: A passage that rewards strategic reading — active noticing, annotation, re-reading of specific sentences, or deliberate self-questioning produces measurably better comprehension than passive first-pass reading
Discrete comprehension-breakdown points in the passage — identifiable sentences or transitions where a passive reader will lose meaning but a strategic reader can catch and recover
Observable signals that cue strategy deployment — a hard sentence, a pronoun reference, a time shift, a tonal shift, a new character introduction — something that should prompt a metacognitive move
A passage complex enough to teach strategy but not so complex that strategy cannot rescue comprehension
mustNotHave: Passages so simple that no strategy is needed — passive reading suffices
Passages so complex that strategy cannot rescue comprehension — metacognition alone is insufficient, other primitives are blocking (vocabulary, syntax, schema)
Passages where the strategic move required is a single domain skill (just inferencing, just tone identification) rather than the general metacognitive monitoring this primitive targets
Paragraphs dominated by dialogue (60%+ quotation marks) where the metacognitive work is character-level rather than reader-level
Nonfiction biographical or memoir prose about real people's lives
Archaic or heavily poetic prose whose strategic demand is inseparable from syntactic parsing
Passages requiring specific historical, political, religious, or cultural knowledge a 9th grader is unlikely to have

tierSignals.tier1: One clear comprehension-breakdown point per passage — an ambiguous pronoun, a time shift, a confusing sentence. Student deploys one strategy (annotate, re-read, clarify) and recovers meaning. Strategic monitoring is focused and bounded.
tierSignals.tier2: Two or three breakdown points across the passage, requiring sustained strategic monitoring. Student must track where meaning is fragile and deploy different strategies per situation — re-read for this one, clarify for that one, annotate for the third.
tierSignals.tier3: Breakdown points are subtle and continuous — the passage requires metacognitive vigilance throughout, not just at marked difficulty spikes. Student must maintain an internal comprehension monitor and deploy strategies proactively rather than reactively.
